summary: Provides methods and settings for IPv6 communication among nodes in range of each other over IEEE 802.11 links operating outside the context of a basic service set, as used in vehicle networks. It needs minimal stack changes and notes limitations. More complex scenarios are left for future work.

eli5.summary: Cars passing each other can talk directly without joining a Wi-Fi network first. This describes how they use internet addresses over such quick links.

questions: what mtu does ipv6 use on 802.11-ocb
subtitle: How ordinary IPv6 runs between cars and roadside units that talk Wi-Fi without ever joining a network.

tldr.problem: Vehicles and roadside units can use IEEE 802.11 radios in OCB mode, where there is no access point, no association and no link-layer encryption. IPv6 needs a baseline for how to run over such links.
tldr.mechanism: IPv6 is layered over 802.11-OCB much as it is over Ethernet (RFC 2464): QoS data frames with EtherType 0x86DD, a 1500-octet default MTU, 64-bit interface identifiers and the standard Neighbor Discovery. The RFC then lists where OCB differs, mainly for subnets, security and privacy.
tldr.outcome: The result is a minimal-change baseline, with the limits written down. Multicast, Neighbor Discovery behaviour and handover are left as open issues for future work.

today: RFC 8691 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2019. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It says it has no IANA actions.

sections.title: Scope and Goal
sections.content:
RFC 8691 gives a baseline for using IPv6 among nodes in range of each other over a single IEEE 802.11-OCB link (also known as 802.11p). The aim is minimal changes to existing stacks, and the RFC also states the limitations of doing so.

The resulting stack is derived from IPv6 over Ethernet (RFC 2464) and provides at least point-to-point connectivity using IPv6 Neighbor Discovery (ND) and link-local addresses. Movement detection, ND extensions and IPWAVE optimizations for vehicular communications are not in scope. The expectation is that further specifications will cover more complex vehicular scenarios.
sections.eli5: It is a starter recipe for putting internet addresses on cars that can talk to each other. Fancy extras are left for later recipes.

sections.title: OCB Mode and the Players
sections.content:
OCB (outside the context of a Basic Service Set) is a mode in which a station is not a member of a BSS and does not use IEEE 802.11 authentication, association or data confidentiality. Appendix B adds that it uses the wildcard BSSID ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, sends no beacon frames, and needs no authentication, association or encryption to communicate.

Two kinds of node appear. An IP-OBU is a computer in a vehicle with at least one IP interface running in OCB mode. An IP-RSU is situated along the road, has at least two IP-enabled interfaces, and at least one of them runs in 802.11-OCB mode. The link model is simply STA --- 802.11-OCB --- STA, and all links are assumed to be point-to-point.

Stations can exchange IP packets only if they are set to the same channel. How a station chooses its channel is not specified in this document.
sections.eli5: Normal Wi-Fi is like checking in at a front desk before you can chat. OCB mode is like two people on a road who just start talking, so both must be tuned to the same radio channel.

sections.title: MTU and Frame Format
sections.content:
The default MTU for IP packets on 802.11-OCB is inherited from RFC 2464 and is 1500 octets. As noted in RFC 8200, every link on the Internet must have a minimum MTU of 1280 octets.

IP packets MUST be sent as QoS data frames. The IPv6 packet is immediately preceded by an LLC header and an 802.11 header, and the LLC Type field MUST be 0x86DD (IPv6). The 802.11 data service mapping SHOULD use a priority value of 1 (QoS with a Background user priority), keeping higher priorities for safety-critical and time-sensitive traffic.

To limit code changes, drivers MAY implement IPv6 over Ethernet as in RFC 2464 and then translate frames from 802.3 to 802.11.
sections.eli5: The message goes in a standard envelope, labelled as an internet message. It is marked as low priority so urgent car-safety messages can go first.

sections.title: Addresses and Autoconfiguration
sections.content:
If an IPv6 link-local address is formed from an EUI-64 identifier, it is formed the same way as on Ethernet. Whatever method is used, the interface identifier (IID) is 64 bits long.

For global or unique local addresses, the RECOMMENDED method for stable IIDs is the one in RFC 8064. The RFC 2464 method MAY be used during transition time, particularly for link-local addresses. IIDs should be treated as opaque. Semantically opaque IIDs, which avoid privacy risks, can be generated with the method of RFC 7217, and using it is RECOMMENDED for stable IIDs that do not change within a subnet prefix.

Address mapping MUST follow Sections 6 and 7 of RFC 2464. Unicast is scoped to address resolution and duplicate address detection per RFC 4862. Multicast mapping follows Section 7 of RFC 2464, but the RFC notes that multicast over 802.11 has known performance issues that may be worse in OCB mode.
sections.eli5: Each car gets a 64-bit name tag for its network address. It is better if the tag looks random, so nobody can read the car maker out of it.

sections.title: Subnets and Neighbor Discovery
sections.content:
Vehicles in close range may form a subnet over their 802.11-OCB interfaces. IPv6 ND requires bidirectional connectivity and, for duplicate address detection and address resolution, transitive properties. An IPv6 subnet can therefore be mapped on an OCB network only if all nodes share a single physical broadcast domain. ND also needs permanent connectivity to defend addresses, which means very stable network conditions.

Vehicle mobility makes the subnet ephemeral, and the hidden terminal effect appears. When timing requirements are very strict (for example, a fast drive through IP-RSU coverage), no on-link prefix should be configured and using only link-local addresses is RECOMMENDED. The same is recommended for a subnet with no default route where the peers are equally qualified.

The baseline ND protocol (RFC 4861) MUST be supported. Appendix I explains that DAD and address resolution cannot be guaranteed over OCB, and points to RFC 8505 as a better fit for wireless links. OCB nodes that support it SHOULD support the 6LN operation. Mobile IPv6 and DNAv6 may need extra tuning, which is left for further study.
sections.eli5: Cars drive in and out of range all the time. The usual way of agreeing who has which address needs everyone to stay put, so often it is simpler for neighbours to use only short-range local addresses.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
OCB does not use the existing 802.11 link-layer security mechanisms, and no encryption is applied below the network layer. Any IP-layer security that works for IPv6 in general may also be used, and IPsec may protect a wider range of applications. IEEE 1609.2 provides application-layer security services for certain applications but is out of scope.

Because there is no association or challenge exchange, an attacker within range can sniff or inject traffic, and may use a sensitive directional antenna, so closeness is not required. Any node can join a subnet and talk directly to the others, including potentially impersonating another node. SEND is named as a solution for spoofing attacks, though it is not widely deployed.
sections.eli5: Since nobody checks ID at the door, anyone nearby can listen in or pretend to be someone else. Important secrets need their own lock.

sections.title: Privacy and Changing Addresses
sections.content:
A vehicle whose interface identifier stays the same can be tracked, since eavesdroppers along roads can correlate the identifier, or the company ID in a MAC address, with other data. The RFC calls for dynamically changing MAC addresses, semantically opaque IIDs and stable IIDs. A vehicle should also renew the IID in its link-local addresses when its environment changes, for example when the engine is running.

When the MAC address of an 802.11-OCB interface changes, all Interface Identifiers of IPv6 addresses on that interface MUST change. A randomized MAC address has the Local/Global bit set to locally administered, the Unicast/Multicast bit set to Unicast and 46 random bits.

Because of this pseudonymization, upper-layer protocols and applications SHOULD NOT rely on layer-2 or layer-3 addresses to assume the other party can be trusted.
sections.eli5: If a car always wears the same name tag, people can follow it around. So the tag should change often, and nobody should trust a tag just because they have seen it before.
